notes.meaning: Elijah proposed a public test to settle who the real God was once and for all. Both sides would place a bull on an altar, and the God who sent fire from the sky to burn the offering would be acknowledged as true. Since the people believed Baal had power over storms and fire, this gave Baal's prophets every advantage on their own home turf. The crowd readily agreed that this was a fair and sensible test.

Elijah told the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal to step forward first because they had the larger numbers. He let them choose whichever bull they preferred, giving them first pick and plenty of time. He told them to prepare the animal and pray to their god, but strictly ordered them not to light any fire themselves.

The prophets of Baal prepared their bull and cried out to their idol from morning until the middle of the day. They shouted desperately for an answer, yet the sky remained silent with no voice and no flame. In their frenzy, they danced and leaped around the altar they had built, trying to persuade a lifeless statue to respond.

At noon, Elijah began to poke fun at the false prophets and their silent idol. He sarcastically told them to shout louder because a real god might be busy thinking, traveling, or taking a nap. His sharp words exposed how foolish it is to trust in a god that has no power to hear or help.

Spurred on by Elijah's mockery, the prophets shouted louder and slashed their own skin with knives and spears. This painful ritual was their custom to try to win their god's pity by shedding their own blood. The true God never demands that His people harm themselves, but false religion often brings cruelty and pain.

The afternoon wore on, and the prophets continued their frantic chanting right up until the time of the evening sacrifice. Despite all their loud noise and wild efforts, there was total silence, with no voice, no answer, and no one paying attention. Their make-believe god had no power to act, leaving them exhausted and exposed as frauds.

Elijah called the crowd to gather around him so they could watch every detail closely. He then rebuilt an ancient altar of the Lord that had been torn down during the rise of Baal worship. By repairing this ruined altar, Elijah showed that he was calling the nation back to the true faith of their ancestors.

Elijah gathered twelve stones to build the altar, with each stone standing for one of the twelve tribes of Israel. Even though the nation had split politically into two separate kingdoms, God still saw them as one covenant family bound to Him. The name Israel reminded the people that their forefather Jacob had wrestled with God in prayer and received His blessing.

Elijah used the twelve stones to build an altar dedicated solely to the Lord. Around the base, he dug a large trench capable of holding several gallons of grain. This deep ditch was made ready to catch the water that would soon be poured out, removing any doubt about what was about to happen.

Elijah placed the firewood in order, cut the bull into pieces, and laid the meat on top. He then ordered four large jars of water to be poured over the wood and sacrifice three separate times, totaling twelve jars. The water soaked everything and filled the trench, proving beyond doubt that no hidden fire or trick was involved.

At the exact time of the evening sacrifice in Jerusalem, Elijah stepped up to the soaked altar to pray. He called upon the Lord as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, appealing to God's ancient promises. He asked God to make it clear that day that the Lord was the only God in Israel, and that Elijah was simply His obedient servant.

Elijah pleaded for God to answer him so that all the watching people would know the Lord is the one true God. The prophet did not ask for personal glory, but prayed that God would turn the hearts of the people back to Himself. True prayer seeks God's honor and the spiritual rescue of others.

Suddenly, fire from the Lord fell from the sky and burned up the sacrifice, the wood, the stones, and even the dirt. The heat was so intense that it dried up every drop of water inside the trench. This miraculous flame left no doubt that the Lord had heard His prophet and accepted the offering.

When the people saw the fire strike the altar, they fell flat on their faces in holy fear and awe. With one voice, they shouted that the Lord alone is God, openly rejecting Baal. Their confession proved they were convinced by the miracle, though they still needed to follow through with true change in their lives.

Elijah ordered the crowd to seize all the prophets of Baal and allow none to escape. The people led them down the mountain to the Kishon valley, where Elijah had them put to death. This severe judgment carried out God's Old Testament law, which required execution for false prophets who seduced Israel into idolatry.

Elijah told King Ahab to go eat and drink because the sound of a heavy rainstorm was approaching. Even though the sky was still clear, Elijah heard the storm coming with the ear of faith. Because the people had turned against the idols, the curse of drought was finally ready to be lifted.

Ahab went to enjoy his meal, but Elijah climbed up to the peak of Mount Carmel to pray in quiet. The prophet knelt down and tucked his face between his knees in deep humility and focus. While the king was feasting, the prophet was pouring out his heart to God for the promised rain.

Elijah told his servant to walk to the ridge and look out over the Mediterranean Sea for any sign of rain. The servant came back and said the horizon was completely empty, but Elijah told him to go back seven times. The prophet refused to give up, showing patient persistence in prayer until the answer came.

On the seventh look, the servant spotted a tiny cloud no bigger than a man's hand rising up from the sea. Elijah knew this small sign meant a huge downpour was on its way, so he sent word for Ahab to prepare his chariot at once. If the king did not leave right away, the coming flood of rain would turn the ground to mud and trap his wheels.

The sky quickly grew black with heavy wind and storm clouds, and a drenching rain began to fall. The terrible drought of more than three years was broken in answer to Elijah's prayers. Ahab rode his chariot through the torrential storm to reach his royal palace in Jezreel.

The Lord gave Elijah supernatural energy and strength. The prophet tucked his long outer robe into his belt and ran on foot through the mud, staying ahead of Ahab's chariot all the way to Jezreel. By running before the king, Elijah showed proper honor to the royal office while proving that God's power rested upon His prophet.
